events.title: TypeScript preview released
events.summary: Microsoft released the TypeScript preview on October 1, 2012 — a typed superset of JavaScript by Anders Hejlsberg.
events.about: TypeScript adds optional static types, interfaces, and generics to JavaScript, then compiles to plain JS. It powers large frontends (Angular, VS Code itself) and Node backends where teams want compile-time checks without leaving the JS ecosystem. `.ts` files catch typos before runtime and enable IDE autocomplete at scale.

narrative.whyChosen: TypeScript became the default for large-scale JavaScript applications and framework tooling.
narrative.whyImportant: It bridged JavaScript's flexibility with IDE support and refactoring safety enterprise teams expected.
narrative.problemSolved: Plain JavaScript lacked types for million-line codebases; teams needed safety without abandoning the web platform.

events.title: Internet Explorer 10 released
events.summary: Microsoft released Internet Explorer 10 on October 26, 2012 with Windows 8 — featuring a touch-first UI, improved HTML5/CSS3, and do-not-track by default.
events.about: IE 10 shipped in two modes: the modern Metro-style browser on Windows 8 and the desktop version for legacy sites. It advanced pointer events, flexbox, and GPU compositing — Microsoft's last major IE push before Edge.

narrative.whyChosen: IE 10 was the touch-era Internet Explorer tied to Windows 8's launch.
narrative.whyImportant: Pointer events and modern CSS support influenced cross-device web standards.
narrative.problemSolved: Windows 8 needed a browser built for touch tablets and hybrid laptops.

events.title: OAuth 2.0 standardized
events.summary: RFC 6749 defined the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework in October 2012 — letting apps request limited access to user accounts without sharing passwords.
events.about: OAuth 2.0 is how you 'Sign in with Google/GitHub' and how APIs delegate access with bearer tokens. Authorization servers issue tokens after user consent; resource servers validate them. Every SaaS integration, mobile login, and third-party API permission screen builds on these flows — authorization code, client credentials, and more.

narrative.whyChosen: OAuth 2.0 replaced ad-hoc API keys and password sharing with a standard consent model.
narrative.whyImportant: It became the foundation for modern identity federation, API security, and OpenID Connect.
narrative.problemSolved: Apps needed user data from other services without storing credentials or getting full account access.
